article.title: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: 6-Question Self-Quiz (I–VI)
article.meta_description: Take a simple Fitzpatrick skin type test, see what types I to VI mean, and learn why it's not the same as skin tone or undertone for makeup and color.
article.h1: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: A 6-Question Self-Quiz and What Your Result Means
article.body_html:
A Fitzpatrick skin type test sorts you into one of six types (I to VI) based on how your skin tends to react to sun: whether it burns, tans, or both. You can estimate your type with the six questions below. The result describes sun reaction only. It does not tell you your skin tone, your undertone, or which foundation and clothing colors suit you.

What the Fitzpatrick scale is (and what it isn't)

A six-type scale based on how skin reacts to sun

The Fitzpatrick scale was developed in the 1970s by a dermatologist as a way to describe how different skin responds to ultraviolet light. Type I sits at one end (skin that burns very easily and barely tans) and Type VI at the other (skin that rarely burns and is deeply pigmented). Types II to V fall in between.

Why it is not the same as skin tone, undertone, or oily/dry skin type

People often mix up four different ideas:

  • Fitzpatrick type: how skin tends to react to sun.
  • Skin tone (depth): how light or deep your skin looks, from fair to very deep.
  • Undertone: the subtle warm, cool, neutral, or olive cast beneath the surface color.
  • Oily, dry, or combination skin: a separate, cosmetic way of describing how skin feels and looks through the day.

Who uses it, and why a self-test is only a rough guide

The scale comes from dermatology, and professionals use it as one reference point. A quiz you score yourself relies on memory and honesty, and most people's reactions don't fit neatly into six boxes. Treat your result as a rough label, not a medical assessment.

Before you start the Fitzpatrick skin type test

Think about your natural, unprotected skin, not a tan or a product

Answer for your skin as it is without a tan, self-tanner, or tinted product. Check an area that rarely sees the sun, such as the inner upper arm.

Answer from experience, not a single holiday

One unusual trip, like a cloudy week or a day with heavy sunscreen, can skew your answer. Think about what usually happens across several years.

A pen-and-paper way to score your answers

Each question below has five options worth 0 to 4 points. Write down one number per question for Questions 1 to 5, then add them up. This is a simplified scoring system for this guide, not a clinical tool.

The self-test: 6 questions to estimate your Fitzpatrick type

Question 1: What is your natural skin color in areas rarely exposed to sun?

  • 0: Very pale or ivory
  • 1: Fair or light
  • 2: Light-medium or beige
  • 3: Olive or light-to-medium brown
  • 4: Deep brown to very deep brown

Question 2: What happens after your first unprotected sun exposure of the season?

  • 0: Always burns, often painfully, and may peel
  • 1: Usually burns
  • 2: Sometimes burns mildly
  • 3: Rarely burns
  • 4: Almost never burns

Question 3: Does your skin tan afterwards, and how deeply?

  • 0: Never tans; goes red or freckles
  • 1: Tans slightly and slowly
  • 2: Tans gradually to a light brown
  • 3: Tans easily to a moderate brown
  • 4: Tans very easily and deepens quickly

Question 4: How do eye and natural hair color fit in? (a loose clue only)

Eye and hair color are the weakest clue, because plenty of people don't match the typical pattern. Score it anyway, but don't lean on it.

  • 0: Red or very light blonde hair, light blue or green eyes
  • 1: Blonde or light brown hair, blue, green, or hazel eyes
  • 2: Brown hair, hazel or light brown eyes
  • 3: Dark brown hair, brown eyes
  • 4: Black hair, very dark brown eyes

Question 5: How does your skin react to repeated sun exposure over time?

  • 0: Stays sensitive and burns again easily
  • 1: Burns less over time but still often
  • 2: Tans, with an occasional burn
  • 3: Tans and rarely burns
  • 4: Deepens in color and doesn't seem to burn

Question 6: Do your answers point to two neighboring types?

Add up your score from Questions 1 to 5 (0 to 20). If the total lands within a point of a band boundary, or your answers are scattered, read both neighboring types in the next section and go with the one that matches your real-life sun history better.

Your result: Fitzpatrick types I to VI in plain language

Total scoreEstimated typeTypical sun reaction (general description)
0–3IBurns very easily, hardly tans
4–7IIBurns easily, tans minimally
8–11IIISometimes burns, tans gradually
12–14IVBurns rarely, tans easily
15–17VVery rarely burns, tans deeply
18–20VIRarely burns, deeply pigmented

Types I and II: skin that tends to burn easily

These types burn quickly and tan little or not at all. Type I is the most sun-reactive, and Type II is slightly less so.

Types III and IV: skin that burns sometimes and tans gradually

Type III tends to burn mildly at first and then tan. Type IV burns less often and tans more readily. These are common middle-of-the-scale results, and they cover a wide range of looks.

Types V and VI: skin that rarely burns and tans easily or is deeply pigmented

These types burn less often, but "rarely" does not mean "never", and it doesn't mean skin needs no sun protection (more on that below).

If you fall between types: why that is normal and what to do

Skin reactions vary with season, climate, and how much sun you've had recently, so landing between two types is common. You don't need to force a single answer. If a professional ever asks for your type, tell them how your skin actually reacts and let them assess it.

Fitzpatrick type vs skin tone vs undertone

A quick comparison: what each one describes and what it is used for

Fitzpatrick typeSkin tone (depth)Undertone
DescribesSun reactionHow light or deep skin looksWarm, cool, neutral, or olive cast
How you find itQuestions about burning and tanningCompare your skin in natural lightVein, jewelry, and white-paper checks
Useful forA general reference point on sun reactionFoundation depth, color contrastFoundation, blush, lip, and clothing colors

To find the last two, see our guides on how to find your skin tone depth and undertone and five simple undertone tests.

Why two people with the same Fitzpatrick type can need different makeup shades

Two people can both score Type IV, with one having a fair, golden-beige complexion and the other a deep olive-brown one. Their foundation shades, and the colors that flatter them, will be quite different. The type only describes sun reaction, so it can't pick a shade.

Where the scale falls short for describing the full range of skin tones

Six types cannot capture the huge variety of real skin tones and undertones, especially among deeper complexions, which get grouped into just a couple of categories. That is another reason not to use it for color decisions.

What to use for makeup and clothing colors instead

Find your depth and undertone

Check your skin in natural daylight near a window, without makeup. Note whether it reads fair, light, medium, tan, deep, or very deep, then work out whether the undertone is warm, cool, neutral, or olive using the guides linked above.

Consider your natural contrast

Contrast is the difference between your skin, hair, and eyes. High contrast (for example, deep hair against fair skin) often carries sharp pairings such as black with crisp white. Low contrast (soft hair and skin tones close together) often looks polished in tonal outfits, like oatmeal with camel or dusty blue with soft gray.

Cosmetic starting points for foundation, blush, lip, and wardrobe colors

  • Foundation: test three shades along the jawline in daylight and choose the one that disappears into your neck.
  • Warm or golden undertones: try peach or terracotta blush and coral or warm brick lips. For clothes, try olive, camel, rust, and cream.
  • Cool or pink undertones: try rose or berry blush and raspberry or mauve lips. For clothes, try navy, emerald, charcoal, and cool pinks.
  • Neutral or olive undertones: you can often move between both families. Try muted greens, plum, and warm taupe, then see which feels best in daylight.

These are starting points, not rules. For more on matching makeup to your features, try our six-question makeup quiz.

Sun protection and skin health: what this test can't tell you

Sun protection matters for every skin tone and type

A low-burn result does not mean you can skip sun protection. Widely accepted general habits, such as sunscreen, shade, and protective clothing, apply to everyone. How much and what kind is a question for a health professional, not a quiz.

A quiz result is not a risk assessment or a medical opinion

This test does not measure sun damage, predict personal risk for any health condition, or replace an examination. A number from I to VI says nothing about the health of your skin.

When to see a dermatologist or doctor

See a dermatologist or doctor about any skin concern, including a mole or spot that changes, new or worrying marks, or questions about professional treatments. They can examine your skin in person, which no quiz or app can do.

Where FitCheck AI fits in

What the live skin analysis does: a cosmetic skin overview with beauty suggestions

If you took this test hoping to choose makeup or colors, FitCheck AI's live skin analysis with your camera gives you an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. The app also has an AI makeup assistant and a live virtual makeup try-on, so you can preview a lipstick shade on your own face. It is an Android app, free on Google Play, and iOS is coming soon.

What it does not do: it does not classify a Fitzpatrick type, diagnose, or give medical advice

The app cannot determine your Fitzpatrick type or assess how your skin reacts to sun. The AI feedback is a starting point, not a professional opinion or medical advice, and anyone with a skin concern should see a dermatologist or doctor.

Photo tips: natural light, eye-level camera, no filters

For makeup and skin looks, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level, and turn off filters. Filters and warm indoor bulbs change how skin and color read on camera.

faqs.question: Is the Fitzpatrick skin type test accurate?
faqs.answer: A self-scored quiz is only a rough guide. It depends on how well you remember your own sun reactions, and many people sit between two types. Treat the result as a loose label, not a medical assessment.

faqs.question: Can the Fitzpatrick type tell me my foundation shade?
faqs.answer: No. The scale describes how skin reacts to sun, not how light or deep it looks or what undertone it has. For foundation, test shades along your jawline in natural light and work out your depth and undertone instead.

faqs.question: Can I be two Fitzpatrick types at once?
faqs.answer: Your answers can sit between two neighboring types, such as III and IV, and that's common. Skin reactions also shift with season and recent sun exposure. Describe how your skin actually behaves rather than forcing a single number.

faqs.question: Do darker skin tones still need sunscreen?
faqs.answer: Sun protection applies to every skin tone and type. Lower-burn skin can still be affected by sun, so general habits like sunscreen, shade, and protective clothing are widely recommended. A dermatologist or doctor can give advice specific to you.

faqs.question: Can an app tell me my Fitzpatrick type?
faqs.answer: FitCheck AI cannot. Its live skin analysis gives a cosmetic overview with beauty suggestions, not a Fitzpatrick classification or medical advice. For anything health-related, see a dermatologist or doctor.

review.notes:
The article meets informational intent. It gives a usable self-quiz, a clear table of types I to VI, and a strong explanation of how Fitzpatrick type differs from skin tone and undertone. All app mentions match APP_FACTS: live skin analysis described as cosmetic, AI makeup assistant, live virtual makeup try-on, Android free on Google Play, iOS coming soon, and the photo tips. It explicitly says the app cannot classify a Fitzpatrick type, and it includes the dermatologist referrals. No invented stats, studies, accuracy claims, or storage/privacy claims.

Minor, optional improvements:
(1) The '6-question' framing is slightly loose, because Q6 is a tie-break instruction and not a scored question. Consider calling it a '5-question quiz plus tie-breaker' or rewording Q6.
(2) The scoring is custom and disclosed as 'simplified, not clinical'. Q1 (skin color) and Q4 (hair/eye color) are pigment clues, not sun reaction, while the intro says the result describes sun reaction only. A one-line note would resolve this. The official Fitzpatrick questionnaire uses a different, longer 0–40 scoring.
(3) Type VI is described as 'rarely burns'. Many sources say it 'never burns' or 'very rarely burns'. The wording is acceptable but could be tightened.
(4) The 'neutral or olive' bullet merges two distinct undertone categories that the article lists separately earlier.
(5) Vein and jewelry undertone checks are of limited reliability. This is fine because the article defers to linked guides.
(6) Verify that the internal links (/blog/..., /ai-skin-analysis/) resolve.
